title: Satellite Images Reveal How Suspected Scam Compounds Appear Out of Nowhere
gist: Satellite imagery analyzed by the International Justice Mission and reviewed by WIRED shows at least 25 new or significantly expanded suspected scam compounds in Myanmar's Myawaddy region since around the start of the year, indicating that Myanmar's televised 2025 crackdown destroyed capacity that has already been more than replaced. Starlink terminals are still detected at roughly half the new sites, and anti-trafficking groups report previously raided compounds have been repopulated with new trafficking victims.

insights.claim: At least 25 alleged scamming sites have been built or significantly expanded in the Myawaddy region of Myanmar near the Thai border since around the start of the year, according to International Justice Mission satellite-image analysis reviewed by WIRED.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Physical build-out is a measurable leading indicator of scam-industry capacity — satellite counts, not government statements, are the honest tracker of fraud volume aimed at Western consumers.
insights.quote: More than two dozen suspected new scam compounds in war-torn Myanmar have been built or expanded significantly in the past six months, according to satellite images and analysis of the area reviewed by WIRED.
insights.locator: Opening paragraph — 'More than two dozen suspected new scam compounds'

insights.claim: The new construction in Myawaddy is large enough to more than absorb the capacity destroyed in Myanmar's 2025 crackdown, according to IJM global analyst Eric Heintz, meaning enforcement disrupted operations without shrinking the industry.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Sanctions-and-raids headlines should not be read as a decline in scam-loss risk for payment, crypto, and social platforms exposed to victim flows.
insights.quote: “While that crackdown did disrupt operations, the scale of these new developments appears to be more than enough to absorb what was destroyed last year.”
insights.locator: Quote from Eric Heintz — 'Some were skeptical that the crackdowns'

insights.claim: Myanmar's military junta staged its compound raids starting around October, ahead of national elections, publicly exploding buildings and steamrolling phones and computers — a sequencing that frames the crackdown as election-timed political display.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Enforcement pegged to an electoral calendar tends not to persist; discount announced host-government crackdowns when modeling fraud-loss trajectories.
insights.quote: Starting around October, ahead of elections in the country, Myanmar’s military junta raided some known compounds, making a show of exploding buildings and steamrolling phones and computers used in the scam operations.
insights.locator: 'The industrial-scale scam operations have turned into a global crisis'

insights.claim: Global Alms Incorporated has drone-confirmed that nine compounds previously believed emptied by raids are populated again with new trafficking victims, per CEO Mechelle B. Moore.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Independent ground/drone verification contradicts official closure claims — a template for how NGOs can be used as an alternative data source on enforcement efficacy.
insights.quote: “We have drone footage, so we’ve confirmed eyes on for nine of the different sites that we thought had been emptied, and they’re all populated, and new victims in there,” she says.
insights.locator: Closing section — 'Moore, of Global Alms, says that despite the crackdowns'

insights.claim: Raiding a compound relocates rather than dismantles the operation because the criminal entities behind the sites are not targeted and simply move people to other compounds, according to Global Alms' Mechelle B. Moore.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Site-level enforcement without financial/ownership attribution is a whack-a-mole cost, not a solution — the durable pressure point is money flows and connectivity providers.
insights.quote: “Nothing has changed, unfortunately,” Moore says. “It's just growing.”

themes.theme: Construction pace as a detection signal

insights.claim: Suspected scam compounds in Myanmar can go from empty fields to operational sites in a couple of months, per IJM analyst Eric Heintz, giving the industry a build-cycle far shorter than any enforcement cycle.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A two-month capacity replacement time means fraud supply is effectively elastic; loss-rate models for banks and crypto exchanges should not assume durable enforcement gains.
insights.quote: “The pace of construction is significant—some of these are going from empty fields to operational compounds in a couple months,” Heintz says.
insights.locator: 'Some of the new and expanding compounds identified by Heintz'

insights.claim: Satellite imagery reviewed by WIRED shows roughly 24 buildings appearing at a single Myawaddy site between January and April, alongside razed forest, new roads, and probable housing built around the compounds.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Building counts per site give a rough headcount proxy for scam labor capacity that can be tracked monthly from commercial imagery.
insights.quote: Satellite images seen by WIRED show how buildings have been created within clearings, with around 24 buildings appearing at one site between January and April.
insights.locator: 'Satellite images seen by WIRED show how buildings'

insights.claim: Clusters of large buildings that are likely accommodation for trafficking victims are a recurring architectural signature across the newly identified compounds, letting analysts classify sites from layout alone.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Layout-matching turns imagery into a scalable classifier — the same pattern-recognition approach applies to other illicit-infrastructure monitoring.
insights.quote: “The layout of these compounds match what we’ve seen in the 30-plus other larger compounds in the area,” Heintz says

insights.claim: Heintz infers the new sites are scam-related from a combination of remote locations with no plausible alternative regional use plus tech data showing a variety of foreign internet service providers at those coordinates.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Fusing geospatial imagery with connectivity/adtech telemetry is a repeatable OSINT method for attributing illicit infrastructure without ground access.
insights.quote: “That, combined with the tech data showing a variety of foreign internet service providers associated with the locations, make me think that these locations are scam-related,” he says.
insights.locator: 'He explains that many of the newly identified sites are in remote locations'

insights.claim: Heintz has previously used mobile advertising industry data to determine which devices and internet service providers are in use at known Myanmar scam compounds, showing commercial adtech exhaust doubles as a criminal-infrastructure tracker.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Adtech location data is a live intelligence channel — a regulatory and reputational exposure for the data brokers whose feeds enable it, and a research tool for investigators.
insights.quote: The researcher has previously used data from the mobile advertising industry to analyze what devices and internet service providers are being used at known scam compounds in Myanmar
insights.locator: 'The researcher has previously used data from the mobile advertising industry'

insights.claim: At least half of the newly identified suspected scam compounds in Myanmar are using Starlink terminals, according to IJM's Eric Heintz, who says the compounds' locations and in some cases the Starlink connection IPs are known.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: A named, identifiable Western satellite operator servicing sanctioned-adjacent trafficking sites is a concrete regulatory and headline risk for SpaceX/Starlink.
insights.quote: “We continue to see Starlink being used, with at least half of these new locations using their terminals—we know exactly where these compounds are, and in some cases know the IPs used by Starlink connections from these compounds, and it remains unclear why the company can’t shut these off,” Heintz says.
insights.locator: 'We continue to see Starlink being used'

insights.claim: Starlink has previously said it cut connections to 2,500 devices linked to scam compounds in Myanmar, yet researchers still detect active terminals at new sites — implying enforcement by the operator is partial or lagging build-out.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The gap between a stated 2,500-device cutoff and continued detection is the kind of discrepancy that invites regulatory action against connectivity providers.
insights.quote: Starlink did not immediately respond to a request for comment but has previously said it has cut connections to 2,500 devices linked to scam compounds in Myanmar.
insights.locator: 'Starlink did not immediately respond to a request for comment'

insights.claim: A prior WIRED investigation found at least eight Myawaddy compounds appearing to use Starlink devices, including rooftop antennas, after which US law enforcement ordered the seizure of Starlink terminals at some compounds.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Journalism-to-seizure precedent shows that public attribution of hardware at these sites can trigger direct US enforcement — a repeatable escalation path.
insights.quote: A WIRED investigation last year found at least eight compounds in the Myawaddy region appearing to use Starlink devices, including having antennas positioned on their rooftops.
insights.locator: 'A WIRED investigation last year found at least eight compounds'

themes.theme: Trafficked labor and the scam economy

insights.claim: Scam compounds across Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos, often run by Chinese organized crime groups, are responsible for vast portions of global online scamming and steal billions of dollars through cryptocurrency and romance scams targeting US and international victims.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Sizes the loss pool that flows through crypto rails and dating/social platforms — the counterparty behind a large share of consumer fraud chargebacks and crypto outflows.
insights.quote: These sites, which are often operated by Chinese organized crime groups, are responsible for vast portions of global online scamming—and are involved in stealing billions of dollars through complex cryptocurrency and romance scams targeting victims in the US and around the world.
insights.locator: 'Over the past decade, scam compounds have appeared widely'

insights.claim: The day-to-day scamming labor — cold-contacting victims on social media, building trust over time, and cashing out stolen money — is performed by human-trafficking victims from more than 60 countries who are held with confiscated passports and beaten if they refuse.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: The forced-labor input means scam supply scales with trafficking flows, not with wage costs — and creates supply-chain/ESG exposure for any firm whose services touch these sites.
insights.quote: People from more than 60 countries have been lured to the region by false promises of work and then forced to scam people 24/7.
insights.locator: 'While overseen by criminal bosses, much of the day-to-day scamming'

insights.claim: Hundreds of thousands of trafficking victims have been tricked into Southeast Asian scam compounds in recent years, making this an industrial-scale labor operation rather than a set of isolated criminal sites.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Scale of this magnitude implies sustained, structural fraud pressure on consumer platforms and payment networks rather than an episodic threat.
insights.quote: Hundreds of thousands of trafficking victims have been tricked into the compounds in recent years.

insights.claim: A raft of international sanctions was issued last year against parties allegedly involved in or linked to the scam operations in Myanmar and Cambodia, yet compound construction continued through and after that sanctions wave.
insights.speaker: Matt Burgess
insights.so_what: Evidence that sanctions on individuals have not constrained physical capacity — expect escalation toward infrastructure, connectivity, and crypto-rail targets instead.
insights.locator: 'The industrial-scale scam operations have turned into a global crisis'
